title: The invisible church
hookLine: enslaved Christians met in secret hush harbors to pray and sing

lines: WET QUILTS AND AN IRON POT.
cards: Servants, obey your masters. On a plantation, that is the sermon from the enslaver's preacher, the one formerly enslaved people would later remember hearing. They sit through it.
Then night comes. One by one, quietly, people slip out of the cabins and into the woods, down to a hollow or a gully where the trees are thick. Someone has hung wet quilts on branches.
Somebody has set an iron pot on the ground, upside down. And there, in the dark, a different church begins. Today: the invisible church.

teach.b: Historians call it the invisible institution, or the invisible church. People who lived it called the meeting places hush harbors. Being caught could mean a beating, so everything was built for silence.

In the memories of formerly enslaved people, written down later, the wet quilts and the turned-over pot come up more than once: ways, they believed, to catch and soften the sound. The preaching there was different.
Some slaveholders' sermons leaned on one line from Paul, in the King James Bible: "Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters."
In the hush harbor, people preached Exodus instead: a God who hears the cry of slaves and brings them out. They preached Jesus, who suffered and rose.
They prayed out loud, called out, moaned, sang, and sometimes shouted, all as quietly as they could. And they sang the songs now called spirituals.
One gives today's line: steal away, steal away to Jesus. On the surface, it's about going to God. Some people say it was also a call to the next secret meeting, and later a hint about escape.
Tradition holds both meanings together, and the song doesn't explain itself.

teach.h: WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.
teach.b: Jesus had said: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." No building, no permission, no preacher hired by the master. Just people in the dark, sure that Christ was with them.
That hidden church is one of the roots of the Black church in America, alongside the churches free Black Christians were already building in the open, like Richard Allen's in Philadelphia.

how: Spirituals like Steal Away are still sung in Black churches, and some congregations remember the hush harbors in services that honor the faith of enslaved ancestors.

games.why: people went, again and again, building their meetings for silence, with wet quilts and turned-over pots to soften the sound.

practice: Find somewhere small and out of the way, a closet, a car, a corner, and let your voice drop to nothing. Remember the people who met in the hollows at night, risking everything just to be together and to sing.
If you pray, pray there in a whisper or without words; if you don't, let the quiet place hold you, and remember them.

wordCard.voice: Hush harbors. The secret meeting places in the woods where enslaved Christians gathered at night to pray, preach and sing their own faith.

orig.note: Greek: an assembly, a gathering — the New Testament word translated church. no building needed.

carryVoice: Your line: steal away. Their church had no walls at all. That's day nine hundred twenty-two.
